comparator.name: Religious Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The Dutch-taught full-time bachelor comprises 60 EC per year, including some English-taught courses. The adopted 2026–2027 programme regulation lists Arabic first among the permitted first-year subject packages; the dated guide specifies its four 6 EC language courses. This neutral illustration retains the common Religious Studies curriculum, 30 EC of open choice and an 18 EC thesis trajectory. It excludes the shortened programme and other first-year packages. The degree has no formal graduation tracks.
components: The first year also requires a Dutch writing diagnostic. Tutoring and study guidance continue throughout the degree. These requirements carry no credits.
Major Questions in Religious Studies 1: Text Analysis
Major Questions in Religious Studies 2: Lived Religion
This example uses the 24 EC first-year Arabic package. Students choose one package in another discipline; this does not create a separate graduation track.
Attend Arabic 1 before Arabic 2. Pass both courses before starting Arabic 3 and 4.
Attend Arabic 3 before starting Arabic 4. The sequence develops Egyptian Arabic and then Modern Standard Arabic.
Religion, Art and Culture 1: Mythology and Storytelling
Secrets of the West 1: Culture and Counterculture before Modernity

Post-first-year courses require a positive binding study recommendation. The ordinary full-time threshold is 48 first-year EC. Complete Secrets of the West 1 before 2, and both before the research project.
Secrets of the West 2: Culture and Counterculture in the Modern Period
Secrets of the West 3: Culture and Counterculture Research Project
Religion and Spirituality in the Netherlands 1: Concepts and Theories
Religion and Spirituality in the Netherlands 2: Lived Religion
Complete Concepts and Theories before Lived Religion, and both before the Netherlands research project. Students use qualitative methods to investigate contemporary religious practice.
Religion, Art and Culture 2: Sacred Stories in Words and Images
Religion and Spirituality in the Netherlands 3: Research Project
Utopias and Visions of the Future
Bachelor’s Thesis Research Project in Religious Studies

Complete the first year and all compulsory second-year courses before starting. Register for the thesis at the same time. A supervisor must approve the research plan before the first thesis section is written.

Use this 30 EC for electives, a minor, an approved exchange or a placement. Normally no more than 12 EC may be introductory; an approved UvA minor or a same-language sequence can permit up to 24 EC. External study requires Examination Board approval. A placement may occupy up to 12 EC; the Religious Studies and Western Esotericism minors cannot duplicate the compulsory curriculum.
The 12 EC thesis follows the 6 EC research project. Complete the first year and compulsory second-year courses, and pass the research project before the thesis can be assessed.

audience.programmeDescription: Students study religious diversity, traditions, texts and practices through historical, literary and social-scientific approaches. They examine contemporary religion and spirituality, Western esotericism and religion in Amsterdam. The reviewed pathway includes first-year Arabic.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR combination studies religious meaning through myth, art, objects and ritual. Amsterdam also teaches several religious traditions, Arabic, lived religion and specialist research in religious studies.

candidates.label: Religion in society, identity, public life and conflict
candidates.reason: Political rights, conflict and identity already contribute to the core. The political alternative moves into general institutions without sustained coursework on religion as a political institution.

candidates.label: Lived religion, spirituality and cultural change
candidates.reason: Philosophy and literature address spirituality and identity, but a separate curriculum in contemporary lived religion would require empirical study of religious communities and practices.

core: The interpretation of sacred narratives, images, rituals and objects
Historical, philosophical and social inquiry into religion
adjacent: The public and political life of religious communities
questions: How do communities express religious meaning through objects, images and stories?

selection.assessment: The verified route includes mythology, sacred images, popular culture and the cultural history of countercultures. The selected programme gives students successive methods to interpret religious narrative, ritual and material culture. Political rights, conflict and identity already contribute to the core. The political alternative moves into general institutions without sustained coursework on religion as a political institution. Philosophy and literature address spirituality and identity, but a separate curriculum in contemporary lived religion would require empirical study of religious communities and practices.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

alternatives.label: Religion in stories, art and material culture
alternatives.labelReason: Myth, religious imagery and ritual in material culture connect the literature, heritage and philosophy sequence.
alternatives.concept: Study how religious stories, art and artefacts express belief and shape communities. Combine comparative mythology, literary interpretation, art history, Greek archaeology and ancient ritual with philosophy and historical and social research.
progression: Foundational literary, art-historical and social inquiry precedes advanced work on interpretation, material heritage and cultural meaning. All six terms meet the course-reference checks.

trace: Close reading of narrative, poetry, symbolism, allegory and drama provides concrete literary methods. These do not alone establish sacred-text traditions or religious authority.
Western painting is related to religious as well as social/political change, with close visual analysis and a painting research paper.
Classical theory, solidarity, identity, othering and inequality develop analysis of social life. The selected content does not document a sociology-of-religion sequence.

Ancient epic, tragedy and confessional writing support comparative interpretation of mortality, community and cultural meaning. The current evidence is not the old blanket claim that this is organised-religion teaching.

Life writing includes spiritual self-fashioning alongside memory, identity, embodiment, trauma and migration. Its interpretive methods support lived meanings but do not constitute empirical lived-religion training.
The official description supports humanist, feminist, Marxist, minority and psychoanalytic interpretations and a research project. Sacred hermeneutics is not inferred from these general methods.
Ancient objects and craft communities are interpreted in relation to religion, status, gender, exchange and environment. Catalogue, drawing and craft inquiry provide real material-culture methods.

Cross-cultural creation and divine narratives, transmission, gender, power and cultural meaning provide the strongest textual bridge. Myth theories, primary materials and research support substantial comparison; no dismissal as merely incidental.

Adaptation theory and close comparative literary/film analysis support relations among narrative, image and medium. The documented research is not necessarily about sacred narratives or religious reception.

Athenian democracy is studied through primary texts, archaeology, art, religion, myth and ritual, with assembly simulation and research. Religious practice is an integral dimension, not dismissed as absent.
Arguments about God, meaning and Buddhist non-self occur within a broad ancient-to-contemporary philosophical introduction.

Western African masks, sculpture and visual traditions are studied through cultural, religious and social meanings. Modernist influence, colonial collecting and restitution form further substantial strands.

The official description supports Renaissance painting, sculpture and architecture and exchanges involving Islamic Mediterranean courts, trade and colonisation. This receives full consideration without inventing detailed doctrines, assessments or a religious-art specialisation.

The official description studies early-democratic Greece through community and material culture. It supports ancient social interpretation; ritual or doctrine is not added beyond what that description states.
Divine command, moral universality, Nietzsche, goodness, death and meaning connect to belief and values; most of the course develops general ethical reasoning.
Greek and Indian agency, foreknowledge, fatalism, responsibility and time support worldview questions. The course is not documented as teaching contemporary spirituality or religious traditions.

Modernity, phenomenology, interactionism, Bourdieu, coloniality and theory-guided empirical interpretation support culture and identity analysis; no religious-studies subject sequence follows automatically.
Trust, solidarity, public spheres, social movements and civil repair support research on collective institutions. A freely chosen religious organisation cannot establish a taught religion focus.
Compares imperial authority, ideology, legitimacy, culture and legacies through sources and an essay. Relevant to religion/power questions but not a continuing religious-history sequence.

The official description supports art historiography, influential authors, aesthetics, interpretation, identity and the discipline’s global challenges. These are useful methods without proving religious subject matter.
Buddhist accounts of non-self contribute to philosophical selfhood alongside neuropsychology, physicalism, AI and experience. This is a genuine connection, not a general Buddhism survey.
Greek and Indian accounts, love, fear, grief, moral and political emotions develop phenomenological and argumentative inquiry. Religious experience is not established as a continuing focus.
Interviews, ethnography, participant observation, coding and qualitative research projects support the target’s fieldwork methods. A religious community focus is not a specified taught requirement.
